newsitem.title: RUSSIA: KREMLIN MUTE ON FEARS YELTSIN TOO ILL FOR SURGERY.
newsitem.headline: KREMLIN MUTE ON FEARS YELTSIN TOO ILL FOR SURGERY.

text.p: A senior doctor preparing President Boris Yeltsin for heart surgery cast doubt on whether the Russian president would survive an early operation, but the Kremlin maintained silence on his remarks on Sunday.

The presidential press office issued no statements and could not immediately be reached for comment. A Kremlin spokesman said on Saturday only that the surgeon's remarks had been distributed "to all the people concerned".
Cardiac surgeon Renat Akchurin said on Saturday that Yeltsin must have suffered a third, and unreported, heart attack just before he was elected in July to a second four-year term.
Akchurin told Reuters that the damage to the president's heart could make the planned bypass surgery too risky and the operation might have to be either postponed or cancelled.
He and other doctors, including U.S. cardiologist Michael DeBakey, will make a final decision next Wednesday or Thursday.

"The most likely decision is that the operation will be postponed," Akchurin told French TF1 television. "In effect, if the risks are high, no one will want to take the chance...A surgeon does not jump off a plane without a parachute."

Russian media treated the surgeon's comments with extreme caution. Some television channels briefly mentioned the remarks without fanfare but neither the official Itar-Tass news agency nor independent agencies reported them.
In a comment on the overall political situation, presidential chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais said it was not time for rivals to try to step into 65-year-old Yeltsin's shoes.

"Those politicians who believe that it is time to take up starting positions in a presidential campaign will very soon realise that they have jumped the gun," Chubais told a congress of the Russia's Democratic Choice party in Moscow on Saturday.
Akchurin told a U.S. television interviewer on Friday that Yeltsin had suffered his third heart attack in about 12 months in late June or early July.

He said later he had not personally treated the Kremlin leader at the time but he concluded from examining Yeltsin's heart later and from considering media reports that a new heart attack had occurred.
His remarks implied that he had not known what he was undertaking when he agreed to conduct the operation, which Yeltsin announced on September 5.
Akchurin's disclosures could worry Western leaders who regard Yeltsin as the guarantor of stability in a vast unpredictable country.
Yeltsin stayed in hospital and out of the public view at the weekend. He has been undergoing tests in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital for more than a week.
A decree on Thursday confirmed that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional deputy, would govern while the president was incapacitated.
But other ambitious and powerful figures, including Kremlin security chief Alexander Lebed, were expected to continue to assert the importance of their own roles in the hierarchy.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, whom Yeltsin defeated in the presidential election, has said that he is now best placed to become the next Kremlin leader. REUTER
